questions.prompt: You have one clarifying question left before designing "something like WhatsApp". Which answer changes the architecture the most?
choices: The maximum group size, and whether broadcast channels with tens of thousands of members exist
Whether messages support emoji reactions and stickers
Which mobile platform ships first
Whether users can pin conversations to the top of their list
questions.explanation: Group size decides the fan-out strategy (per-member inbox copies are affordable at 256 members, not at 100,000), whether per-member receipts make sense, and whether channels need fan-out on read, digests and time-bucketed partitions. Reactions and stickers are small messages on the same path. The first platform changes the client, not the system. Pinning is a client-side or inbox-attribute feature with no architectural weight.

questions.prompt: At 50 M DAU, which non-functional requirement adds the most components to a chat design?
choices: The number of simultaneously open connections
The average message size
The total number of messages per day
The five-year retention period
questions.explanation: ≈ 10 M open connections force a stateful gateway tier, a session registry, heartbeats, a drain and reconnect plan and admission control: more boxes than any other requirement. Messages per day size the partitioned store and the fan-out, which matters, but a partitioned store is one box on the diagram. Message size and retention change storage arithmetic and tiering, not the set of components on the message path.

questions.prompt: The PM says end-to-end encryption ships next year and asks what you can build now without a redesign later. Select ALL the server-side capabilities that keep working once message bodies are ciphertext.
choices: Per-conversation sequence numbers and gap detection
Dedupe of retried sends by client message id
Server-side full-text search over message bodies
Delivered and read receipt cursors
Keyword-based content moderation on the server
Link previews generated by the server
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers, client message ids and receipt cursors are metadata: the server assigns or stores them without reading the body, so ordering, idempotent sends and receipts are unchanged under E2E. Search, keyword moderation and server-generated previews all need plaintext on the server and disappear (or move to the client). The design lesson: treat the body as opaque bytes from day one and never build a guarantee that depends on reading it.

questions.prompt: The interviewer relaxes one requirement: each device may show messages in its own arrival order, and members need not agree. Which part of the design does this let you remove, and what do you lose with it?
choices: The single writer per conversation that assigns dense seqs; you lose gap detection and unambiguous "read up to N" receipts
The session registry; deliveries can be broadcast to every gateway instead
Dedupe by client message id; arrival order makes retries harmless
The push-notification path; offline devices can sort messages on reconnect
questions.explanation: Without a shared order, nobody has to choose one: the store needs only a unique, roughly increasing id per message. But dense seqs are also what let a client notice a missing message and what make a read cursor mean something, so catch-up and receipts get weaker. The registry is about finding sockets, not order. Retries duplicate regardless of ordering, so client-id dedupe stays. Offline members still need a wake-up signal, so push stays.

questions.prompt: 50 M DAU each send ≈ 40 messages per day. What is the average send rate? Answer in sends per second.
questions.explanation: 50 M × 40 = 2 × 10^9 sends per day; ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23k sends/s (the napkin 2 × 10^9 / 10^5 = 20k is within tolerance). At a 3× peak that is ≈ 70k writes/s, 10–70× what one relational primary does for small transactional writes, so the message store is partitioned by conversation from day one.

questions.prompt: Peak sends are ≈ 70k per second and each message reaches ≈ 2.5 recipient devices on average (1:1 dominates, some groups, some users with two devices). What is the peak delivery rate? Answer in deliveries per second.
questions.explanation: 70k × 2.5 ≈ 175k deliveries/s. Spread across ≈ 40 gateways that is ≈ 4k/s published to each gateway's channel. Roughly half of deliveries go to offline devices, which is why the push service sits beside the design. Using sends instead of deliveries undersizes fan-out by 2.5×.

questions.prompt: ≈ 10 M connections are open at peak, each costing ≈ 30 KB of memory (goroutine stack, TLS and bufio buffers, kernel socket buffers). How much memory does the fleet need for connection state? Answer in GB.
questions.explanation: 10^7 × 30 × 10^3 B = 3 × 10^11 B ≈ 300 GB. Unremarkable across ≈ 40 boxes (≈ 7.5 GB each), fatal on eight (≈ 36 GB on a 32 GB box, the opening failure story). The 30 KB figure is a planning assumption that varies with runtime and TLS settings, so you'd measure it before committing to a box count.

questions.prompt: 10 M concurrent connections; one gateway can hold ≈ 500k; you plan for 50% utilisation plus two spares. How many gateway servers? Answer as a count of servers.
questions.explanation: 10 M ÷ 500k = 20 at 100%; at 50% utilisation, 40; plus 2 spares, ≈ 42. Answering 20 or 22 forgets headroom: when one box dies, its clients must land on the others without pushing them over, and each box is then a blast radius of ≈ 250k users. The tier is sized by connections, not by messages per second.

questions.prompt: 2 × 10^9 messages per day at ≈ 200 B each as stored, replicated 3×, kept for 5 years. How much storage at year five? Answer in PB.
questions.explanation: 2 × 10^9 × 200 B = 400 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 146 TB/year raw; × 3 ≈ 440 TB/year; × 5 ≈ 2.2 PB. Forgetting either replication or retention is off by 3× or 5× (15× together). The decision: an append-mostly partitioned store with a cold tier after ≈ 90 days; storage, not the gateway fleet, becomes the dominant cost line.

questions.prompt: 10 M open connections each heartbeat every 30 s. How many heartbeat frames per second does the fleet handle? Answer in frames per second.
questions.explanation: 10^7 ÷ 30 ≈ 333k frames/s fleet-wide, ≈ 8k/s per gateway on ≈ 40 boxes. At ≈ 100 B on the wire that is ≈ 270 Mbps for the whole fleet, so bandwidth is irrelevant; the costs are a little CPU and, on the phone, battery. The interval is a NAT-timeout and battery decision, not a bandwidth one.

questions.prompt: A deploy restarts the whole gateway fleet, holding 10 M connections, within 3 minutes, and every client reconnects. What reconnect rate do auth and sync see? Answer in reconnects per second.
questions.explanation: 10^7 ÷ 180 s ≈ 55k reconnects/s, each a TLS handshake, a token validation, a registry write and a sync call. An auth service sized for ≈ 20k logins/s collapses, clients retry, and the fleet flaps (a metastable failure). The same restart over 60 minutes is ≈ 2.8k/s, which is why deploy speed is a capacity decision.

questions.prompt: A colleague says each gateway can hold at most ≈ 65k WebSocket connections "because there are only 65,535 ports", so 10 M users need ≈ 150 gateways. What is the right correction?
choices: The server accepts every connection on one port and the 4-tuple distinguishes them; the real limits are file descriptors, memory per connection, TLS CPU during reconnect waves and conntrack tables on middleboxes
The claim is right: each accepted connection consumes a server port, so only more IP addresses per box raise the limit
The limit applies only to TLS connections; plain TCP sockets are unlimited
The limit applies only to IPv4; moving clients to IPv6 removes it
questions.explanation: The ≈ 64k figure is ephemeral source ports per source IP for *outbound* connections (it bites a proxy dialling one backend from one IP), not a cap on accepted connections. Accepted sockets share the listening port; what you actually hit is ulimit/fs.file-max, memory (≈ 30 KB × 500k ≈ 15 GB), handshake CPU during waves and nf_conntrack_max on stateful middleboxes. TLS and IPv6 have nothing to do with port exhaustion on the server side.

questions.prompt: Your sheet assumes ≈ 20% of 50 M DAU are online at peak. During a global sports final it is 50%. Which line of the estimate sheet moves the least?
choices: Five-year message storage
Gateway count
The reconnect wave of a full-fleet restart
Session registry entries and heartbeat refresh rate
questions.explanation: Concurrency drives everything about the connection tier: gateways (≈ 105 instead of ≈ 42), connection memory, registry entries and their refresh rate, and the reconnect wave (≈ 140k/s for a 3-minute restart) all scale by ≈ 2.5×. Storage depends on messages sent, and people read more than they write during an event, so it barely moves. Connections and messages scale independently, which is why the sheet estimates both.

questions.prompt: A member on a train sends "yes, go ahead". The request times out after 10 s and the app retries; the first attempt had in fact been stored. What makes the retry safe?
choices: The client generates a message id before the first attempt and reuses it; the server dedupes on (conversation, sender, client id) atomically with the insert and returns the original seq
The server dedupes on sender and body within a 5-second window
The server generates the message id and returns it in the ack, so the client can resend with that id
The client retries only on 5xx responses, never after a timeout
questions.explanation: Only an id that exists before the first attempt lets the retry refer to it; dedupe atomic with the insert (a unique index, or one lock) means two racing retries can't both store. A body window drops a member who really sends "ok" twice and misses a retry that arrives after 10 s anyway. A server-generated id is in the ack that was lost, so the client never has it. A timeout and a 5xx are equally ambiguous about whether the write happened; refusing to retry turns a stored message into a lost one from the user's point of view.

questions.prompt: Clients catch up with GET /messages?since=<server timestamp>. Two chat-service nodes have clocks 30 ms apart. Which symptom does this produce, and what removes it?
choices: A message stored later can carry an earlier timestamp and fall behind a device's cursor forever; switch to after_seq with a per-conversation seq assigned by one writer
Messages arrive twice; tighten NTP to 1 ms
Nothing, as long as the comparison is >= and the client dedupes by timestamp
Order is wrong but nothing is missed; sort by UUIDv7 ids instead
questions.explanation: Node A (fast) stores message 1 at .130, a device syncs past .130, node B (slow) stores message 2 at .110: it is behind the cursor and never returned. A seq from one writer has no cursor a later message can fall behind. Tighter NTP shrinks the window but never closes it (ties and skew remain). >= re-fetches ties but can't recover a later write with an earlier stamp, and dedupe by timestamp merges two distinct messages from the same millisecond. UUIDv7 embeds a server's generation time: the same clock problem, and the symptom is loss, not only order.

questions.prompt: Which key design fits the messages table for 1:1 chats and groups of up to 256?
choices: Primary key (conversation_id, seq), partitioned by conversation_id and clustered by seq
A global auto-increment message_id, partitioned by a hash of message_id
Primary key (sender_id, sent_at), partitioned by sender_id
Primary key (recipient_user_id, sent_at), one copy per recipient, partitioned by recipient
questions.explanation: The access patterns are the tail of one conversation, after_seq catch-up and before_seq history: all one-partition range reads on (conversation_id, seq). A global auto-increment is a ≈ 70k/s hot row that also scatters a conversation across partitions. Partitioning by sender turns every conversation read into a scatter-gather over its members, and sent_at is not an order. Per-recipient copies are the per-user inbox sequence: write amplification × members and no single order of record, defensible only when groups are tiny and catch-up by user matters more.

questions.prompt: You're choosing transports for a product with a mobile app, a receive-only web wallboard for a support team, customers behind corporate proxies that block protocol upgrades, and partner bots. Select ALL the sound choices.
choices: WebSocket for the mobile app: one connection carries sends, deliveries, receipts and presence
SSE for the wallboard: plain HTTP with automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID
Long polling for the clients behind the restrictive proxies
Plain HTTP with an Idempotency-Key header for bots, with a cursor poll or a signed webhook for replies
WebSocket for the bots, because only WebSocket delivers messages reliably
gRPC bidirectional streams for the wallboard, because browsers speak gRPC to servers natively
questions.explanation: Transport is chosen per client type. The app wants one bidirectional socket; the wallboard only receives, so SSE is simpler; long polling survives proxies that block upgrades; bots send a few idempotent requests and get replies by cursor or webhook. WebSocket gives a byte stream while the connection lives, not delivery guarantees; reliability comes from the store and the client's cursor. Browsers need gRPC-Web through a proxy, so gRPC streams are a native-client and service-to-service choice.

questions.prompt: A member's phone clock is a full day fast. In the module's design, what goes wrong?
choices: Nothing in ordering or sync: seq and sent_at are assigned by the server; the phone may show its local time on pending bubbles only until the ack arrives
Every message the member sends sorts above everyone else's for a day
The member's sync skips a day of messages because its cursor is ahead
Dedupe fails because client message ids embed the phone's clock
questions.explanation: No client time is used for order or catch-up: seq comes from the conversation's single writer, sent_at from the server, and the sync cursor is a seq. Sorting above everyone is exactly the bug of ordering by client timestamps, which this design avoids. A seq cursor can't be ahead because of a clock. Client ids are random or device + counter and only need uniqueness per sender, not correct time.

questions.prompt: The dedupe key for sends is (conversation_id, client_msg_id). Two different members' devices generate the same client_msg_id and send into the same group within a second. What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: The second message is silently treated as a retry of the first and acked with the first's seq; scope the key by sender: (conversation_id, sender_id, client_msg_id)
Both are stored because the bodies differ; no change is needed
The server returns 409 Conflict and the second client picks a new id; no change is needed
Both are stored with the same seq; add a timestamp to the key
questions.explanation: Dedupe never looks at the body, so the second sender gets an ack for someone else's message and theirs is lost. Client ids are generated independently by each device, so scoping by sender keeps one sender's retry from suppressing another's message. The server can't tell a collision from a retry, so a 409 path doesn't exist without the sender in the key. A seq is assigned once per stored message and never shared. A timestamp in the key breaks the retry itself, because each attempt carries a different time.

questions.prompt: When does the sending device receive its ack in the module's design, and what does the ack promise?
choices: After the message is assigned a seq and durably written to a quorum of replicas, before fan-out; it promises "stored and ordered", not "delivered"
As soon as the gateway receives the frame; durability follows asynchronously
After the bus has published the frame to every recipient's gateway
After at least one recipient device returns a delivered receipt
questions.explanation: Acking after the quorum write is honest (a crash cannot lose an acked message) and fast (≈ 10 ms server-side). Acking at the gateway means a crash before the write loses a message the sender saw as sent. Waiting for the bus ties the ack to a best-effort path and adds latency for no guarantee. Waiting for a delivered receipt makes every send to an offline recipient "fail"; delivery is reported later by a separate receipt.

questions.prompt: The chat service writes message seq 42 to the store, then its pod is killed before it publishes to Bob's gateway. Bob is online. What happens?
choices: Bob gets 42 at his next sync trigger (seq 43 arriving reveals the gap, a latest_seq hint in a heartbeat response, or an app open); if that delay is unacceptable, drive fan-out from an outbox written with the message
The message is lost and Alice must resend it
The per-gateway bus redelivers it when the pod restarts, because the bus holds the durable copy
Alice's device notices the missing delivered receipt and resends with a new client id
questions.explanation: The store is the truth and the push is a hint: the message is durable and acked, so Bob's client recovers it by syncing from its cursor, triggered by gap detection, a latest_seq hint or the next open. An outbox row in the same transaction, processed by a worker that retries, upgrades the push guarantee at the cost of an extra write and a worker tier. Nothing is lost, so Alice has nothing to resend. The bus is deliberately best-effort and never saw the frame. Receipts drive UI, not resends, and a new client id would create a real duplicate.

questions.prompt: Bob's phone comes back after an hour offline. In which order should it act?
choices: Connect the socket first, then sync from its cursors, deduping anything that arrives both ways by (conversation, seq)
Sync from its cursors first, then connect, so that nothing arrives twice
Connect only: the gateway replays everything missed while offline
Sync only, then poll every few seconds until the user opens a conversation
questions.explanation: Connecting first closes the window: anything stored after the sync's snapshot arrives on the socket, possibly also in the sync, and dedupe by seq removes the overlap. Syncing first leaves a gap in which a message stored between the sync and the socket is neither returned nor pushed until the next message or sync. A gateway holds only a bounded queue for live sockets and has nothing for a device that was gone. Polling is the design the module starts by rejecting.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the components that hold state in the module's send-and-sync design.
choices: Gateways: which sockets they hold and a bounded send queue per connection
Session registry: user and device to gateway, with a TTL
Message store: per-conversation log, membership, receipt cursors, inbox
Presence store: online and typing as soft state with a TTL
Chat service: validates, sequences through the store, fans out
Push dispatcher that hands offline deliveries to APNs/FCM
questions.explanation: Sockets, the user → gateway map, the log and soft presence are state. The chat service is deliberately stateless: seq is assigned in the store's atomic write, not in its memory, so it can deploy freely while the socket tier deploys rarely. The push dispatcher is a stateless hand-off to the notification system (C7); content is never relied on from the push.

questions.prompt: An early version used the load balancer's sticky-session cookie as the record of where each user is connected. After the first gateway deploy, messages for reconnected users keep going to the old gateway. What should replace the cookie?
choices: An explicit session registry (user, device → gateway) with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats, or deliberate route-by-hash on an L7 balancer
Broadcast every message to every gateway and let each one filter
A longer cookie lifetime so affinity survives deploys
Holding sockets in the chat-service pods so the sender's pod writes to the recipient directly
questions.explanation: Fan-out needs to ask "where is Bob now"; a registry entry rewritten on every connect and expiring with the heartbeat TTL answers it, and route-by-hash is the defensible alternative when you control L7 routing. Broadcasting is ≈ 42 × 175k ≈ 7 M mostly irrelevant frames/s. A longer cookie lifetime makes the stale mapping last longer. Sockets in the business-logic tier make every deploy a reconnect wave and you still need to find the right pod.

questions.prompt: Gateway 3 dies, dropping ≈ 250k sockets, and messages for those users keep arriving for the next 30 seconds. What does the design rely on so that none are lost?
choices: Every message is durable in the store before it is acked; clients reconnect with jittered backoff to other gateways and sync from their cursors
Gateway 3 persists its per-connection queues to local disk and replays them on restart
The chat service retries publishing to gateway 3 until it comes back
Senders' devices keep messages until a delivered receipt arrives, then resend
questions.explanation: Delivery never depended on gateway 3: the log has every message, the registry entries expire with the TTL (or are overwritten by new connections), and the first sync after reconnect returns the gap. Senders kept getting acks throughout. Replaying from local disk ties users to a dead box and duplicates what the store already has. Retrying publishes to a dead gateway wastes work on a best-effort path. Resending on missing receipts creates duplicates and confuses receipts with delivery.

questions.prompt: You drain one gateway holding ≈ 250k users per minute. Close frames with reconnect-after hints plus client jitter spread its reconnects evenly over ≈ 60 s. What reconnect rate does one drained gateway create? Answer in reconnects per second.
questions.explanation: 250,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 4.2k reconnects/s, under a ≈ 10k/s auth and sync budget. One gateway per minute takes the 42-box fleet ≈ 42 minutes, versus ≈ 55k/s for a 3-minute full restart. The product sees nothing at ≈ 4k/s and goes down at ≈ 55k/s; resumable sessions make each reconnect cheaper and allow faster waves.

questions.prompt: The mobile SDK reconnects every 1 s after a disconnect, and during a deploy the fleet flaps for 40 minutes. Which client policy fixes the shape of the wave?
choices: Exponential backoff with full jitter, capped (≈ 1 s doubling to ≈ 60 s), reset only after a healthy period, honouring server reconnect hints and Retry-After
A shorter fixed interval of 100 ms, so clients find a healthy gateway sooner
Exponential backoff without jitter, so every client waits a well-defined time
Reconnecting immediately to a different gateway picked from a client-side list
questions.explanation: Backoff reduces the rate, full jitter de-synchronises clients, the cap bounds recovery time, and server hints let the fleet shape its own load. A shorter fixed interval multiplies the storm. Backoff without jitter keeps millions of clients in lockstep, producing waves at 1, 2, 4 s. Picking another gateway changes where the load lands, not how much of it there is; auth and sync are still flooded.

questions.prompt: What should set the heartbeat interval on a mobile chat connection?
choices: The shortest idle timeout of NATs and proxies on users' networks, traded against the battery cost of waking the radio
Fleet bandwidth: heartbeats must stay under ≈ 1% of gateway egress
The operating system's TCP keepalive default, which already detects dead peers
The registry's write capacity, because every heartbeat is one registry write
questions.explanation: The heartbeat keeps NAT mappings alive and finds dead sockets, so it must be shorter than the most aggressive idle timeout in the path; every ping costs battery, which pushes the other way (≈ 30–60 s is typical). Bandwidth is ≈ 270 Mbps for the whole fleet, irrelevant. TCP keepalive is usually far too slow by default and tells the application nothing. Registry refreshes are batched per gateway (≈ 42 bulk writes/s), so they don't constrain the interval.

questions.prompt: A phone behind a dead NAT mapping still looks connected, and its per-connection send queue on the gateway is full. What should the gateway do with the next frame for that connection?
choices: Drop it for that connection, count the drop, and send a resync hint or close the socket; the client syncs from its cursor
Block the fan-out until the queue drains, so the frame isn't lost
Grow the queue, because memory is cheaper than losing a message
Return an error to the sender so they can retry later
questions.explanation: The message is already in the store, so dropping a push loses latency, never data, and the client recovers by syncing. Blocking stalls the fan-out (under the conversation's lock, every sender to that group) behind one phone. An unbounded queue turns hundreds of thousands of zombie sockets into a gateway out of memory. The sender's message was stored and acked; telling them to retry would create a duplicate attempt for a recipient-side problem.

questions.prompt: In labs/c6/chat a subscription has a buffer of 8 and never reads. 1,000 messages are sent to its conversation. Under the drop-when-full policy, what must the subscription's Dropped() report? Answer as a count of messages.
questions.explanation: The first 8 offers fill the buffer and every later non-blocking offer fails, so 1,000 − 8 = 992 are dropped and counted, and the 1,000 sends finish immediately. A Sync from seq 8 returns the other 992 from the log. A blocking send would hang the test (the 9th offer never completes); an unbounded slice would report 0 drops and grow without limit.

questions.prompt: After a full-fleet restart, every client reconnects within a few minutes and receives a 1-hour access token. If gateways simply close each socket when its token expires, what happens an hour later, and what is the better design?
choices: Millions of sockets close within the same few minutes and recreate the reconnect wave; clients refresh the token in-band before expiry, the re-auth close is only a backstop, and expiries are staggered
Nothing: token expiry only matters at the next connect
Clients are logged out permanently; issue 30-day tokens instead
The registry entries expire with the tokens, so fan-out stops for an hour
questions.explanation: Synchronised issuance means synchronised expiry, so closing at expiry replays the storm an hour later. An in-band refresh frame avoids the reconnect; the server-side close with a re-auth code remains for clients that don't refresh; jittered lifetimes break the synchrony. Ignoring expiry means a revoked user keeps receiving messages. 30-day tokens widen the theft window to avoid an engineering problem. Registry TTLs follow heartbeats, not tokens.

questions.prompt: Your Connect starts one goroutine per subscription that waits on <-ctx.Done() and then closes the subscription. The cancellation tests pass, but the leak test still finds goroutines after 100 subscriptions are closed, half by cancelling their context and half by calling Close. Why, and what fixes it?
choices: Subscriptions closed with Close leave their goroutine parked on a context nobody will cancel; use context.AfterFunc, or select on both ctx.Done() and a done channel that Close closes
The race detector adds goroutines of its own; run the leak test without -race
Close would have to cancel the caller's context, which it cannot do, so the leak is unavoidable
The buffer is too small; a larger SubscriberBuffer lets the goroutines exit
questions.explanation: A goroutine that waits only on ctx.Done() lives as long as the context, and an explicitly closed subscription's context may live for the life of the process: on a gateway that is ≈ 250k parked goroutines after a day of ordinary disconnects. context.AfterFunc registers cleanup without a goroutine; a done channel closed by Close (once, via sync.Once) gives the goroutine a second way out. The race detector doesn't create those goroutines. Close doesn't need the caller's context. Buffer size has nothing to do with a goroutine waiting on a context.

questions.prompt: During a rolling deploy a phone's socket drops; 20 s later it reconnects to another gateway presenting its session id and the last seq it saw per active conversation. With resumable sessions, select ALL the work this reconnect can skip.
choices: A full token validation, if the session was authenticated recently and the token is not near expiry
A full inbox walk: missed events are replayed from the last seen seqs instead
TCP and TLS setup to the new gateway
Updating the registry to point at the new gateway
questions.explanation: A session resume within its TTL trusts the recent authentication (re-validating only near expiry) and turns the sync into "replay from seq", which is what makes a 42-minute rolling deploy invisible. The new gateway is a new TCP connection with its own TLS handshake; TLS session resumption can shorten that, but it is a separate mechanism and still a handshake. The registry must point at the new gateway, or fan-out keeps publishing to the old one.

questions.prompt: Suppose every server's clock were perfectly synchronised. Why would you still need a single writer per conversation to assign order?
choices: Two sends can be simultaneous to any precision; one party must choose an order once and record it so every member renders the same one
You wouldn't; the single writer exists only to save the storage cost of timestamps
Because timestamps cannot be used as a clustering key in a wide-column store
Because vector clocks would order concurrent sends correctly but are too large to attach to every message
questions.explanation: "Which came first" has no answer for concurrent sends until someone decides it, and every member must see the same decision; the single writer is that tie-breaker, recorded with the durable write. Clocks only add skew and ties on top. Storage is not the reason. Timestamps can be clustering keys; they just don't give an agreed order. Vector clocks leave concurrent events unordered by design, which is exactly the case that needs deciding.

questions.prompt: A client holds conversation X up to seq 41 and receives a frame carrying seq 43. What should it do?
choices: Treat it as a gap: sync after_seq=41 from the store (or render 43 and fill in 42 when it arrives), never silently skip 42
Render 43, because 42 was probably deleted
Hold everything and wait on the socket until 42 arrives
Ask the sender's device to resend 42
questions.explanation: Dense seqs make a missing number a fact, and the store is the truth, so the client fetches the gap. Deletion is a tombstone message with its own seq, so a gap never means "deleted". The push path is best-effort and 42 may never come on the socket. The sender's device has nothing to do with it: 42 is already stored and acked.

questions.prompt: Conversations are owned by lease-holding sequencer nodes. Node A's lease expires during a long GC pause while it is writing seq 42; node B takes over, reads max(seq) = 41 and assigns 42 to a different message. What prevents two messages with seq 42?
choices: Each write carries the lease's fencing token; the store rejects tokens older than the newest it has seen, so A's write fails and its client retries through B, deduped by client id
Node A checks that its lease is still valid immediately before writing
Synchronised clocks make lease expiry exact, so A stops in time
Recipients dedupe by seq, so the second 42 is harmless
questions.explanation: Only the store can arbitrate between owners, and the fencing token is how: the stale owner's write is refused. A check before the write is a race with a pause right after the check. Clocks can't make a paused process notice anything. Dedupe by seq would silently drop a *different* message that happens to share the number, which is loss, not dedupe.

questions.prompt: In the lab you move the dedupe lookup outside the conversation lock: look up, unlock, lock again, append. 20 concurrent retries with one client id sometimes store 2–20 messages, yet go test -race reports nothing. Why?
choices: It is a logical check-then-act race: every memory access is still under a lock, so there is no data race to detect, but two goroutines can both miss the key before either inserts
The race detector only works with -count=1
The dedupe map must be a sync.Map; a plain map hides races from the detector
The lock should be an RWMutex so that lookups can run concurrently
questions.explanation: The race detector finds unsynchronised memory access, not broken invariants. Lookup and insert must be one atomic step: one lock in the lab, a unique constraint on (conversation, sender, client id) in SQL. -count=20 is how you shake out the interleaving, not something that disables detection. Swapping in sync.Map with a separate Load and Store keeps the same gap between check and act. An RWMutex for lookups makes concurrent misses more likely, not less.

questions.prompt: The product spec says, in bold, "messages are delivered exactly once". What can the design honestly promise?
choices: At-least-once transport on every hop, with the server deduping sends by client message id and clients deduping deliveries by (conversation, seq), so each message is shown exactly once
Exactly-once transport, because WebSockets run over TCP and TCP never duplicates
Exactly-once via a two-phase commit between the store and every recipient device
At-most-once delivery with no retries, so nothing is ever duplicated
questions.explanation: Exactly-once is an end-to-end property built from at-least-once plus idempotence at the two ends. TCP dedupes within one connection, but client retries, republishes and reconnect-then-sync duplicate across connections. A two-phase commit with phones that go offline for days blocks forever. At-most-once breaks "nothing acknowledged is lost".

questions.prompt: Select ALL the statements about receipts in the module's design that are correct.
choices: The read cursor is per (conversation, user) and only ever moves forward
The delivered cursor is per device, because delivery is a fact about a device holding the bytes
In a 200-member group the sender's UI shows counts built from coalesced cursor updates
A message rendered in a lock-screen notification preview counts as read
A late receipt from a user's second device may move the read cursor back to keep devices consistent
Receipts are needed for correctness: a message is re-sent when its delivered receipt doesn't arrive
questions.explanation: Reading is a fact about a person (it also clears the badge on their other devices); delivery is a fact about a device; groups get counts, not per-member frames. A notification preview is not the user viewing the conversation, and calling it read is a classic bug. Cursors never move backwards: a late, lower receipt would make the badge flicker and the sender's UI regress. Receipts feed UI and audit; correctness comes from the store and the client's sync.

questions.prompt: A 200-member group sends one read-receipt frame per message per reader, fanned out to every member. How many receipt frames does a single message produce once everyone has read it? Answer as a count of frames.
questions.explanation: 200 readers × 200 recipients = 40,000 frames for one line of text: quadratic in group size. Receipts as cursors per (conversation, user), coalesced every few hundred milliseconds and shown as counts in groups, cost ≈ 200 small updates per reading session instead.

questions.prompt: A group has members in two regions, and the product asks for each region to ack sends locally. Which design keeps "everyone sees the same order"?
choices: Home the conversation in one region whose sequencer orders every send; members in the other region pay one cross-region hop (≈ 80–150 ms) on their acks
Run a sequencer in each region and merge the two sequences by timestamp
Run a sequencer in each region and merge them with vector clocks so concurrent sends get one order
Use one global sequencer for every conversation in the product
questions.explanation: A total order needs one writer per key; homing each conversation keeps that and makes the cost explicit (remote acks are slower). Merging by timestamp gives someone the wrong order. Vector clocks leave concurrent sends unordered, so you end up with a DAG and conflict rules (Matrix) and clients that briefly disagree. A global sequencer is a needless bottleneck and single point of failure because order is only needed per conversation. If the product insists on local acks, say the price: per-region order with visible reorders.

questions.prompt: The app queues sends while offline and retries them for up to 24 hours. The server's dedupe entries expire after 10 minutes. What happens, and what is the fix?
choices: A retry arriving after 10 minutes for a send that was stored is treated as new and duplicated; keep the key at least as long as the retry window (≈ 24 h TTL) or as a unique index on the messages table
Nothing: the client message id makes retries safe whatever the server's TTL
The late retry is rejected with an error and the user sees a failed message
Recipients catch the duplicate because they dedupe by seq
questions.explanation: A client id is only as good as the server's memory of it. Size the TTL from the client's retry policy (≈ 100 B × 2 × 10^9 sends/day ≈ 200 GB live at 24 h), or make the unique index part of the message row and drop the TTL. The server can't reject what it no longer recognises. The duplicate is stored with a new seq, so recipients' seq dedupe shows it twice.

questions.prompt: A user returns after two weeks offline and is a member of 300 conversations. What does a good reconnect look like?
choices: One sync with the inbox cursor returns the conversations that changed (latest_seq, preview, unread), paged; the client fetches after_seq only for those with news, on-screen ones first; a device far behind is told to reload
300 parallel after_seq calls, one per conversation
One response that streams every message from every conversation since the user's last-seen timestamp
No sync: the gateway replays every missed frame when the socket connects
questions.explanation: The inbox cursor turns "what changed anywhere" into one bounded, paged call; per-conversation fetches happen only where latest_seq exceeds the local cursor. 300 calls is 300 round trips and 30 s of spinner for mostly unchanged conversations. An unbounded stream keyed by a client timestamp has both the size problem and the clock problem. Gateways keep only bounded queues for live sockets and have nothing for a device that was gone two weeks.

questions.prompt: 1,000 channels each have 50,000 members and post 10 times a day. With fan-out on write (one inbox write per member per post), what is the average inbox-write rate from these channels alone? Answer in writes per second.
questions.explanation: 1,000 × 50,000 × 10 = 5 × 10^8 writes/day; ÷ 86,400 ≈ 5.8k/s. The average looks harmless; the damage is that each post is a 50k-write burst at once, competing with every other conversation's sends. That burst, not the average, is why channels above ≈ 1k members fan out on read.

questions.prompt: Why is the fan-out-on-write threshold (≈ 1k members) set by bursts rather than by daily averages?
choices: Each post into a large conversation is one inbox write per member, all at once; below ≈ 1k members that is at most ≈ 1 s of store work, above it the spike hurts other conversations even when the daily average looks fine
Daily averages and bursts are always within 3× of each other, so either can be used
Large groups post more often than small ones, so their average is what grows
The threshold is set by storage cost, which depends only on bursts
questions.explanation: A 256-member group at ≈ 1 message/min is ≈ 4 inbox writes/s, trivial; a 50k channel at 10 posts/day averages little but lands 50k writes per post in one go. It is the C5 celebrity decision keyed by conversation instead of author. A 3× peak factor describes diurnal traffic, not a single post's fan-out burst. Member count multiplies the cost of every post, whatever the posting frequency, so frequency is not what sets the threshold. Inbox rows are small; IOPS and latency during the burst decide, not storage.

questions.prompt: A conversation crosses the fan-out threshold and becomes a 50,000-member announcement channel. Select ALL the changes the design makes for it.
choices: No per-member inbox rows at write time: members read the channel row's latest_seq and the tail when they open it
Push notifications become rate-limited digests instead of one per post per member
Per-member read receipts become counts, sampled or dropped
Its partition is bucketed by time so one busy channel never becomes one unbounded partition
Its messages stop being sequenced, because members only read the tail
Every member gets one immediate push per post, so nobody misses an announcement
questions.explanation: Above the threshold the channel fans out on read, notifications become digests (C7 rate limits), receipts become counts and the partition is (conversation_id, bucket). Sequencing is unchanged: the channel still needs one order and gap detection, and its seq is what members' cursors point at. One push per member per post is the 50k-push flood the threshold exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: A user has 5,000 contacts. How should their app learn who is online?
choices: Subscribe to presence only for the ≈ 20 users on screen (the open chat, the visible page of the list); presence is soft state with a TTL ≈ the heartbeat; last seen is pulled when a conversation opens
Receive every presence change of all 5,000 contacts over the socket
Poll the presence of all 5,000 contacts every 10 s
Read presence from the message store, where online and offline transitions are persisted
questions.explanation: Subscriptions bound presence fan-out by what a screen can show, not by the size of the contact list. Pushing all contacts' changes multiplies frames by the contact count; polling 5,000 contacts every 10 s is 500 lookups/s for one user (200 M/s across 10 M users with 200 contacts each). Presence is soft state refreshed by the gateway; persisting every transition to the message store turns a green dot into durable writes.

questions.prompt: 10 M online users each change presence ≈ 20 times a day. If every change were published to all of the user's ≈ 200 contacts, how many presence frames per second would the fleet send? Answer in frames per second.
questions.explanation: 10^7 × 20 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 2.3k changes/s; × 200 contacts ≈ 460k frames/s, more than the ≈ 175k peak message deliveries. With subscriptions (≈ 10 subscribers per change) it is ≈ 23k/s. Typing indicators without throttling add more on top, which is why they get a ≈ 3 s TTL, a per-sender throttle and only members with the conversation open.

questions.prompt: Messages are end-to-end encrypted. A user adds a new laptop. What does the laptop see after its first sync, and why?
choices: Seqs, cursors and receipts as usual, but no readable history unless an existing device re-encrypts it for the laptop, because the server holds only envelopes it cannot decrypt
Full readable history, because the server re-encrypts stored messages with the laptop's key
Nothing: sequence numbers are encrypted too, so sync cannot work
Full readable history, because inbox previews are stored in plaintext
questions.explanation: Under E2E the server syncs ciphertext per device or per group session, so a new device needs a device-to-device history transfer. The server has no keys and so cannot re-encrypt anything. Seqs, cursors and receipts are metadata and keep working. Plaintext previews are exactly what E2E removes; the inbox carries counts only.
